drafts.subject: Re: Prospective GSoC contributor - where to start?
drafts.message:
Hi Fatima!

Thanks so much for reaching out — it's great to hear you're interested in contributing to Jaseci ahead of GSoC. Getting started early is exactly the right move, and your Python background plus the fact that you're already learning Jac from the docs puts you in a strong spot.

Here's a quick roadmap to get you going:

1. **Explore the repositories:** The main org lives at github.com/Jaseci-Labs. Good starting points include:
   - **`jaseci`** — the core runtime and compiler (Python-heavy, great for understanding the engine).
   - **`jaseci-ai-kit`** — a collection of AI/ML models and modules; a nice fit if you're interested in applied AI.
   - **`jac_core`** — if you want to dig deeper into the Jac language implementation.

2. **Look for good-first-issues:** Filter issues by the `good first issue` and `help wanted` labels across the repos. These are intentionally scoped for newcomers and are a great way to make your first PR.

3. **Read the contributing guide:** Each repo has a `CONTRIBUTING.md` (or similar) in the root — it walks through the dev setup, coding conventions, and PR workflow. Start there before opening a PR.

4. **Join the community:** We have an active Discord where contributors, mentors, and maintainers hang out. It's the fastest way to ask questions, get unblocked, and meet potential GSoC mentors. You can find the invite link in the README of any of the main repos or on the Jaseci website.

5. **Engage early:** Even before GSoC applications open, making a small contribution (a doc fix, a good-first-issue, or helping another contributor) helps you build context and shows the team you're committed — something mentors definitely notice when reviewing proposals.

If you tell me which area interests you most (core runtime, AI kits, Jac language, docs, etc.), I can point you to specific issues or repos. And once you're on Discord, drop a note in the contributors channel — folks will be happy to help you get set up.

Welcome aboard, and good luck!

Best,
The Jaseci Team

drafts.subject: Re: Bug: edge traversal returns duplicates after node delete (repro attached)
drafts.message:
Hi Omar,

Thanks for the detailed report and the clear repro—this is very helpful.

1. Known issue? Yes, this is a known issue on our side. When a node is deleted, the edges connected to it are not currently fully cleaned up from the adjacency/index structures of neighboring nodes, so [-->] traversal can surface stale edge references (and, in some cases, duplicates). It's tracked internally as a graph-consistency bug affecting edge lifecycle management around node deletion. It has been observed by a couple of other users as well, though your repro is the cleanest we've seen.

2. Workaround to ship while a fix lands? The most reliable workaround today is to explicitly delete the edges incident to a node before deleting the node itself. In your repro, instead of deleting B directly, remove edges A->B and B->C first, then delete B. This prevents stale references from lingering in A's adjacency. If you can't restructure deletion order easily, a fallback is to post-filter traversal results by edge/node existence—e.g., after [-->] traversal, drop any returned edge whose endpoints no longer resolve to live nodes (or deduplicate by edge ID). The explicit-edge-deletion approach is the one we'd recommend for production since it keeps the graph consistent.

3. GitHub issue? Yes, please do file it. A GitHub issue with your full repro snippet (and the version pin to 0.10.2) will help us track this properly and prioritize the fix. Please also note in the issue that the explicit-edge-deletion workaround avoids the symptom—our team can confirm and reference it when the fix is reviewed.

We'll link the internal ticket to the GitHub issue once it's filed. Thanks again for the proactive report and for being willing to contribute the repro.

Best,
Jaseci Core Team

drafts.subject: Re: Press: quote on agentic programming languages (deadline Aug 5 EOD)
drafts.message:
Hi Grace,

Thanks for reaching out. Happy to provide a quote for your piece.

On-record quote from Jaseci:

"General-purpose languages treat agents as external add-ons, forcing developers to stitch together frameworks and libraries for capabilities that should be first-class—autonomous traversal, typed LLM delegation, and persistent graph state. Agent-native languages like Jaseci build these concepts directly into the language, eliminating the abstraction leaks and integration friction that make agentic software fragile and hard to scale."

You're welcome to attribute this to a Jaseci spokesperson or contact me for attribution specifics.

Best of luck with Thursday's article.

Best,
Jaseci Team
impact@jaseci.org
